where: Section 3, position-based routing paragraph (and exam trap 3)
problem: Perimeter mode of GPSR is described as forwarding 'around the void using the road graph'. In the standard definition, GPSR perimeter mode forwards on a planarized graph of the radio neighbours (Gabriel graph or relative neighbourhood graph) using face routing / the right-hand rule. It is the positions of neighbours, not the road layout, that define the faces. Students will reproduce a wrong mechanism.
fix: At a local maximum no neighbour is closer, so perimeter mode forwards the packet around the void by face routing on a planarized graph of the radio neighbours, using positions taken from GPS.

problem: The lead says a VANET works 'with no fixed base station', then Section 1 introduces the RSU, a fixed access point. A reader can take these as contradictory.
fix: Say in the lead that links form as cars meet and that RSUs beside the road are optional fixed access points; the network still works without them.

problem: 'Greedy forwarding ... guarantees delivery only after perimeter mode' reads as an unconditional guarantee. Delivery is guaranteed only when the network graph is connected and has been planarized, and the destination lies in the same connected component.
fix: Greedy forwarding can stop at a local maximum; perimeter mode then recovers, and delivery is guaranteed only if the neighbour graph is connected and planarized, as GPSR assumes.
